name: Focus page
description: One task on the whole screen with the application chrome removed: a bag scanned into a GRN at the gate, a bin counted at a rack, a sample passed or failed at the QC bench. Large targets, type one step up, and a scan field that never gives up the keyboard.
when_to_use: A tablet bolted to a trolley or held in a gloved hand, a barcode gun in the other, and one action repeated a few hundred times a shift — receiving bags into GRN-4821, counting rack B-14, passing or failing a sample at the bench. Three things have to be true together: the operator is standing rather than sitting, the screen does exactly one thing, and the input is a scanner or a gloved thumb rather than a keyboard and a mouse. This is one of the only signed-in screens in the library that does not render inside app-shell, and the exemption is narrow on purpose. The shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark, the command palette and the keyboard shortcuts, so dropping it is only paid for where the chrome is actively harmful — where a 68px rail is 68px of target taken off a screen read at arm's length, and where a link to another part of the application is a route to losing a count nobody has posted yet. Every other signed-in screen is app-shell, including the ones that feel simple; the test is not "this page is focused", it is "the operator has one hand free and must not be able to wander off". The same figures typed at a desk are form-page — a keyboard, a mouse, the 13px scale and a validation summary — and that is the right screen for the supervisor amending the GRN an hour later. A QC checklist worked through in full and countersigned is questionnaire; this entry is one of its questions, at a bench, at bench scale, and a run of eighteen of them belongs back in questionnaire where they can be read as a column. A queue somebody walks while keeping the queue on screen is list-detail.
rules: This is the exception to the rule that every signed-in screen is app-shell, and the exception has to be paid for rather than assumed. Dropping the shell drops the skip link, the nav landmark, the off-canvas trap, the palette and the shortcuts, so the screen supplies by hand the two of those it genuinely needs — a <main> landmark and exactly one route out — and deliberately supplies none of the rest. If a screen wants the shell back for anything at all, it wanted app-shell.

Type goes up one step across the whole screen, and that is a decision rather than drift. Nothing here is smaller than 13px: the default is 16px where the rest of the library runs 13px, secondary lines are 14px where the library runs 12px, section headings are 16px, and the one value the operator reads at arm's length — the scanned code, the counted quantity, the running total — is 24px, the top of the scale. An 11px uppercase label under a work light on a tablet propped a metre away measures as accessible and cannot be read, so this screen has no 11px and no 12px type on it at all.

Targets go up with the type. Controls are h-12 at the smallest, h-14 for anything the operator reaches for repeatedly and h-16 for the one thing the screen is for, against the 36–44px the shape token gives the rest of the library. 44px is the floor for a finger on a phone held still; it is not the floor for a gloved thumb on a trolley that is moving. Keypad keys and answer tiles are bigger again, because they are hit without looking.

The h1 is the smallest heading on the screen and that is deliberate. On a page with no chrome the title is the least useful thing on it — the operator knows which station they are at — so it takes the 20px section step and the task takes the 24px page step. The heading outline is still correct: one h1, regions under it as h2.

The scan field holds focus by taking it back on blur, and the blur handler reads relatedTarget before it does. A barcode scanner is a keyboard: with focus anywhere else the scan lands in the wrong control or in no control at all, and the operator finds that out three racks later. Anything the operator is allowed to move the keyboard into carries data-hands-off — the manual-entry box, Finish, Exit — and everything else is pulled back on the next animation frame. The alternative, a document-level keydown handler that redirects characters into the field, was rejected: it swallows the operator's own typing, it cannot tell a scanner from a keyboard, and it breaks the moment a dialog opens.

The first focus of the page is taken on $nextTick, not in x-init directly. x-init on a component root runs before Alpine has walked its children, so $refs.scan does not exist yet and the call is a silent no-op — the screen loads looking ready, the operator scans, and the first read of the shift goes nowhere. It is the same class of defect as focusing a control that is still display:none, and it fails in exactly the same way: measurably correct, visibly nothing.

inputmode="none" on the scan field is load-bearing, not an omission. Focusing a text input on a tablet raises the on-screen keyboard, so a field that always has focus means a keyboard permanently covering half the screen; the hardware scanner types into it regardless of what the input mode says. The manual-entry route flips to inputmode="text" because there the soft keyboard is the point.

Loudness on this screen is size, not colour. A refusal is a 24px sentence in black on white with one red icon beside it, exactly the alert shape the rest of the library uses — a red field behind the message would be visible from further away and would say less, and it is the first thing forced-colours mode repaints. The audible half of a refusal belongs to the scanner, which beeps differently for a good read and a rejected one; the page does not make sound.

A rejection recovers without the operator touching the screen. The field is already empty and still holds the keyboard, so the next scan replaces the message — nothing has to be dismissed. A refusal that needs an OK press costs the operator a hand they do not have, and after the third one they leave a finger resting on the button and stop reading.

Keypad keys prevent default on mousedown so the pointer never moves focus off the quantity field. That is the pointer half only: a tap on a touch screen still moves focus, which the field's own blur handler takes back, and a Tab to a key is a deliberate keyboard move that is left alone.

A run counter is derived from the answers, never incremented. Going back to amend rack 11 must not decrement the total, because rack 11 still holds a figure — the count moves only when a rack gains or loses one. A counter that steps down on Back and up again on Record drifts every time somebody checks their work, and the drift is invisible until the numbers are reconciled at the end of the shift.

A stock count hides the system figure until the operator has committed theirs. Shown first, the count stops being a count and becomes a confirmation of the number already on screen, and the variance the whole exercise exists to find is the one thing it can no longer produce.

Nothing destructive sits within a thumb's width of the commit target. The commit is the full width of the column at the bottom edge where the hand already is; Back, Exit and anything that discards are at the top of the screen or separated by a rule, because two 64px targets 8px apart on a moving trolley is one mis-tap.

Offline, the screen states what is true rather than what is comforting: how many scans are held on this tablet, that none of them is in the GRN, and that closing the tab loses them. It also states what stopped working — the item lookup, so a bag that would have been refused is now accepted into the queue and may be refused when the queue goes up. A queue that lives only in memory has to say so on screen; if the deployment persists it, that sentence changes and nothing else does.

There is exactly one route out and it is guarded. With no sidebar and no breadcrumb, Exit is the only in-app navigation on the screen, so it is the only place the unsaved-work dialog has to live — and beforeunload covers the tab being closed, which on a shared tablet is how work is actually lost. With nothing in hand Exit does not raise the dialog at all, or people learn to press Discard without reading it.

The snippet root is a fixed-height frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the exit dialog is absolute inset-0 against it. As a real page it is h-dvh on a bare document that does not extend the app-shell base: drop the wrapper border, make the dialog fixed inset-0, and let the middle band be the only thing that scrolls.

anatomy.description: The one band of chrome: which station this is, which document is open, whether the tablet is on the network, and Exit. It is a <header>, because with no shell nothing else claims the banner landmark, and it is never a topbar — it carries no navigation and no search.
The h1, at the 20px step. It names the document being worked on and nothing else; the line under it carries the item, the lot and the unit.
One 64px field at 24px, permanently focused, inputmode="none". The gun types the code and presses Enter. It is the only control on the screen that takes the keyboard by default.
The named way to type instead — a button carrying data-hands-off that swaps the scan field for a keyed one at inputmode="text". Escape returns the keyboard to the scan field.
The permanent role="alert" panel under the field whose text is replaced on every scan. Accepted, refused, or held — one icon, one 24px sentence, one line saying what to do next.

The last few reads, newest first, so the operator can check the gun is reading the right label without waiting for the total. Server rows are real markup; scans made since load are prepended above them.
The figure and the progress rail at the foot: how many of the known total are done. Derived from the answers, so amending one does not move it.
A 3-by-4 grid of 64px keys for a quantity typed with gloves on. Keys prevent default on mousedown so the pointer never takes the keyboard off the field they write into.
questionnaire's three-tile answer at bench scale — equal columns, a real radio inside each, the tint painted by has-[:checked]. Position carries the verdict, so Fail is always the middle target.
The full-width 64px primary at the bottom edge. It states what is about to be written above itself, and nothing destructive is within reach of it.
What is held on the tablet while the network is down: the count, the oldest entry, and the sentence saying none of it is saved.
The alert-dialog raised by the only route off this screen, naming exactly how much uncommitted work is in hand and offering to post it rather than only to keep or discard it.

behaviour: The scan field is focused on load and takes focus back whenever it loses it, unless the keyboard moved into a control marked data-hands-off. The re-focus runs on the next animation frame, so it does not fight the click that caused the blur.

Enter is the scanner's terminator, not a submit. It reads the field, records the code, clears the field and leaves focus where it is; the form is never submitted by the gun, because a navigation would take the keyboard with it.
A refused scan clears the field, leaves the running count alone and says so. The next scan replaces the message, so recovery costs no touch; nothing has to be dismissed and nothing times out.

The manual route swaps the scan field for a keyed one rather than adding a second field beside it. There is one field on screen at a time, so there is never a question of which one the gun is typing into. Closing it returns focus to the scan field after a tick and a frame, because a control that is still display:none cannot be focused.

A keypad key writes into the quantity field without taking the keyboard off it. The pointer is prevented from moving focus, and a tap that moves it anyway is pulled back by the field's own blur handler.

A stock count reveals the system figure and the variance only after the operator commits their number, and the reveal is a status region rather than an alert — it is the answer to something they just did, not an interruption.

Going back in a run reopens the previous position with its recorded figure already in the field and says that recording again replaces it. The completed count does not move, because the position it went back to still holds a figure.

Offline, scanning keeps working and the queue grows. Anything that would need the server — the item lookup, posting the document — is unavailable and says why in a sentence beside it rather than only by being dead.

Exit is the only in-app navigation on the screen. With uncommitted work it raises the guard; with nothing in hand it leaves immediately. beforeunload covers the tab being closed, and a successful post clears the flag before it navigates.

Only the middle band scrolls. The station strip and the commit bar are fixed at the two edges, so the commit target is in the same place whether the echo list has two rows or forty, and nothing on this screen scrolls sideways at 390px.
accessibility: One <main> and one <h1>, both supplied by this screen rather than by the shell. The station strip is a real <header> so the banner landmark exists, and the commit bar is inside <main> because the action belongs to the task and not to the frame.

The scan field has a real visible <label>, never a placeholder standing in for one. The placeholder says what the field is waiting for and disappears the moment anything is in it, which is exactly when a screen reader user most needs the name.

The outcome panel is a permanent role="alert" whose text is replaced on each scan, not a panel that is inserted and removed. A live region that arrives with the page announces nothing, and one that is created and destroyed announces unreliably; replacing the string inside a region that was already there is what actually reads.
The reveal after a stock count is role="status", not role="alert". It answers something the operator just did, and an assertive interruption would talk over the control they are still standing on.

The progress rail is role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a name pointing at the figure already on screen. It is not a live region — announcing the total after every scan is a sentence read three hundred times a shift.

Every bound number is paired with the server's figure written into the element underneath it. A count that exists only as x-text is a hole in the sentence until Alpine boots, and on a tablet at an unloading bay that is not instant.

Answer tiles are real radios inside their labels, so the tile is the target and the label text is the option name. The criterion is referenced with aria-describedby from every option rather than from the fieldset, because focus lands on one radio and only that radio's description is read.

A quantity field driven by a keypad is still a real input with inputmode="numeric", so a keyboard user types into it directly and the keys are an alternative rather than the only route. Each key is a button with its own accessible name; the backspace key is named rather than left as an icon.

A control that is genuinely unavailable is disabled and carries the reason as text beside it. A dead button on a screen with no other affordances tells the operator nothing at all about what to do next, and there is no menu here for them to go looking in.

The exit dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, x-trap.noscroll and Escape bound, and it returns focus to the control that opened it. It is the only modal this screen has, and with no shell there is no focus trap anywhere else to inherit.

{{ grn.item.name }} · lot {{ grn.lot }} · {{ grn.pack_kg }} kg a bag · {{ grn.vendor.name }}

{% comment %} The form posts one code and swaps one panel. autofocus wins the first paint before any script runs; the hx-on handler holds it after every request. Both are needed — autofocus alone loses the field on the first swap, and the handler alone leaves the field cold until the operator scans once into nothing. {% endcomment %}
{% csrf_token %}

The gun types the code and presses Enter. The spinner sits beside the field, never on it.

{% comment %} Permanently in the document and never removed, so replacing its text is what announces. A live region inserted by the swap that creates it announces nothing at all in most screen readers. {% endcomment %}

Tailwind compiles its stylesheet out of the literal strings in the source, so a class of w-[{{ pct }}%] scans as the token w-[{{ and emits no rule at all — the rail comes back empty, which renders as a bug rather than as an error and is why it ships. {% endcomment %}
